1.pericope_label: The salutation: Paul an apostle by the will of God, and Timothy our brother

schools.summary: Gill makes the assertion of apostleship partly defensive, since the false teachers everywhere insinuated that Paul was not an apostle, and partly a claim to authority, to give the greater sanction to what he should say, to command the greater regard, and to excuse his freedom in writing to a church he had never seen, he being the apostle of the Gentiles; he notes that Paul had seen Christ in person and received his commission, doctrine and qualifications immediately from him, with a power of doing miracles to confirm his mission, and that he was sent not by men but by Christ. Calvin argues that because the Colossians had never seen him his private name by itself was not sufficient, so he premises that he is an apostle of Christ set apart by the will of God, from which it follows that he did not act rashly in writing to persons not known to him, since he was discharging an embassy God had entrusted to him and was not bound to one church merely, his apostleship extending to all; and he notes that the term applied to the readers is the more honourable, by which Paul allures them the more willingly to listen to him.

Henry defines an apostle as a prime-minister in the kingdom of Christ, immediately called by Christ and extraordinarily qualified, whose work was peculiarly to plant the Christian church and confirm the Christian doctrine, and observes that Paul attributes this not to his own merit, strength or sufficiency but to the free grace and good-will of God, holding himself engaged to do his utmost because he was made an apostle by that will. He finds in the joining of Timothy another instance of Paul's humility, and marks that though he elsewhere calls him his son he here calls him his brother, which is an example to the elder and more eminent ministers to look upon the younger and more obscure as their brethren and to treat them with kindness and respect; and on the titles given the readers he says that towards God they must be saints, consecrated to his honour and sanctified by his grace, bearing his image and aiming at his glory, and towards one another brethren standing in a near relation and owing a mutual love, and that in both they must be faithful.

Clarke prefers a different spelling of the city's name from that which Barnes adopts, places it in Phrygia, seated on an eminence on the south side of the Maeander near the place where the Lycus enters the earth and runs underground for about three-quarters of a mile before emerging and falling into the greater river, and sets it between Laodicea and Hierapolis at an equal distance from either. He traces its rulers, the Macedonians transferring it to the Persians, then the Seleucids, then the king of Pergamus after the battle of Magnesia, and at last the Romans when the last of that line bequeathed them his dominions, so that with the whole of Phrygia it formed part of the proconsular province of Asia until the time of Constantine, after which Colosse was the sixth city of the first division of a divided Phrygia; and he notes that the government of the city had been democratic, its first magistrate bearing the title of archon and praetor, and that Xerxes came there on his expedition against Greece.

Barnes gives a full account of the situation of the city, in the southern part of Phrygia, east of Ephesus and north of Laodicea, and traces its fortunes through the ancient authors, a great city to one, well inhabited and pleasant and large to another, but by a later geographer reckoned among the smaller towns; he records that in the latter part of Nero's reign, not long after this epistle was written, Colosse together with Laodicea and Hierapolis was overwhelmed by an earthquake, that it recovered so far that the Byzantine writers count it among the most opulent cities, and that the ancient town is now extinct though its site is occupied. Ellicott observes that except in the mention of Timotheus the salutation is almost verbally coincident with the opening of the epistle to the Ephesians, and that the naming here against the omission there marks the difference in character between the two epistles, since in a special epistle like this Timotheus would be joined with St Paul as usual, whereas in a general epistle to the churches of Asia the Apostle alone could rightly speak. Robertson denies that Paul describes himself because of any attack, as in Galatians, holding rather that he does so because he is unknown to the Colossians, and observes that the order of the two names in the later epistles shows that Christ is now regarded as a proper name and not merely a verbal adjective; he takes the mention of Timothy as a function of where Paul happened to be.

Chrysostom observes that though all Paul's epistles are holy, some advantage belongs to those he sent after he was in bonds, and reckons this one among them since Paul writes in it that he is in bonds; he places it after the epistle to the Romans, since that was written before Paul had seen them and this after, and near the close of his preaching. His evidence is Onesimus: in the epistle to Philemon Paul calls himself the aged and makes request for him, whereas in this he sends Onesimus himself, calling him the faithful and beloved brother; and he adds that Paul could here say boldly that the gospel had been preached in all creation under heaven, which required that it had by then been preached a long time. He puts the epistle to Timothy later still, written when Paul was come to the very end of his life and could say that he was already being offered, and the epistle to the Philippians earlier than this one.

debates: Why Paul asserts his apostleship: Gill makes it partly defensive against teachers who insinuated he was no apostle, Robertson denies any attack and grounds it in his being unknown at Colosse, Calvin argues the same way and adds that it showed he did not write rashly to strangers, and Henry attributes the office itself wholly to the free grace and good-will of God

Why Timothy is named: Henry finds an instance of humility and a lesson to elder ministers in the word brother, Ellicott a mark of the letter's special as against general character, contrasting the omission in the epistle to the Ephesians, and Robertson simply a function of where Paul was

What the city was called and what became of it: Barnes and Clarke prefer different spellings and different sources, Barnes stressing the earthquake under Nero that overwhelmed Colosse with two neighbouring cities not long after the epistle, and Clarke the succession of its rulers and the underground course of the river

When the epistle was written: Chrysostom places it after the epistle to the Romans and near the close of Paul's preaching, arguing from Onesimus being requested in one letter and sent in this, and from the gospel having by then been long preached
outliers: Chrysostom's principle that some advantage belongs to the epistles Paul sent after he was in bonds
Chrysostom's argument from Onesimus, requested by letter in one epistle and sent in person with this one

Clarke's note that the river enters the earth near the city and runs underground about three-quarters of a mile before emerging
Clarke's account of the city's democratic government, its first magistrate bearing the title of archon and praetor

Robertson's inference from the order of the two names that Christ is now regarded as a proper name and not merely a verbal adjective

2.pericope_label: The saints at Colosse, the salutation, and the thanksgiving

schools.summary: Gill denies four things about the saints before he affirms anything: they are holy not by birth, since all are unholy and unclean by nature, nor by baptism, which neither takes away sin nor gives grace, nor merely externally by an outward reformation; but by separation, being set apart for God in eternal election, by imputation, Christ being made sanctification to them, and by the sanctifying grace of the Spirit in regeneration, having principles of grace wrought in them and being formed as new men in righteousness and true holiness; brethren, as born of God and of his household; and faithful, as true and sincere believers, constant and persevering in the faith of Christ and in their profession of the gospel. Calvin asks why the letter opens with thanks rather than compliment, and observes that Paul makes use of thanksgiving in place of congratulation, by which he teaches us that in all our joys we must readily call to remembrance the goodness of God, since everything pleasant and agreeable to us is a kindness conferred by him, and that he admonishes us by his example to acknowledge with gratitude not merely what the Lord confers upon us but also what he confers upon others; he adds that in praising their faith and love Paul both encourages them to alacrity and constancy of perseverance and procures their friendly regards, so that they may be the more favourably inclined and teachable for receiving his doctrine, and that in thanking God for both graces he acknowledges both to be conferred by God, since otherwise the gratitude were pretended.

Henry lays down the rule broadly, that thanksgiving ought to be a part of every prayer, and that whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving; he notes that in his prayers for them Paul gave thanks for them, that in our thanksgiving we must have an eye to God as God and as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, in and through whom all good comes to us, and that it is a matter of encouragement in all our addresses that we can look to him as Christ's Father and our Father, as his God and our God; and he says the thanks are given for the graces of God in them, which were the evidences of the grace of God towards them.

Clarke disposes of the word saints in five, that they were those who professed Christianity; he reports that many excellent manuscripts, both the Syriac and other versions, and a string of fathers give a different spelling of the city's name from the received one and judges that most probably the true reading, adds on the authority of an early historian that the city perished by an earthquake a short time after the date of this epistle, and names the village supposed to occupy the site; and on the salutation he reports that the clause naming Christ is omitted by many manuscripts, several versions and some of the fathers, and that an editor left it out of the text, but says plainly that in his opinion the evidence was not sufficient. Wesley divides the two titles between the two relations, the first expressing their union with God and the second their union with their fellow Christians, and notes that there is a near resemblance between this epistle and those to the Ephesians and the Philippians.

Barnes turns aside in his introductory notes to the letter from Laodicea which Paul directs the Colossians to read, observing that the most natural and obvious interpretation is that Paul had sent a letter to that church also and wished them to procure it, that no such epistle is now extant, and that much difficulty has consequently been felt in determining what he referred to, so that he canvasses the several opinions entertained, the first being that the reference is to a letter sent from the Laodiceans to Paul. Robertson says the spelling of the city's name is uncertain, the manuscripts differing between the title of the letter and the text of this verse, and describes the valley, whose tributary streams carried a calcareous deposit of a peculiar kind that choked them and made arches and fantastic grottoes, yet left much fertility in the valley with two prosperous cities within ten or twelve miles; he quotes another that this was the least important church to which any of Paul's epistles were addressed and answers that Paul had no greater message for any church than the one he gives here concerning the Person of Christ; he accepts the shorter text of the salutation and notes that this is the only opening benediction in the epistles where the name of Jesus Christ is not joined with God our Father; and he notes that the word rendered always stands amphibolously between the giving of thanks and the praying and may be taken with either. Ellicott holds that the best manuscripts give the salutation simply as from God the Father, varying from Paul's otherwise universal phraseology, and that such a variation can hardly be accidental; he asks whether it may have been suggested to the Apostle's mind by his special desire in this epistle to emphasize the true Godhead of Christ, an instinctive reluctance to use any phrase, however customary with him, which might even seem to distinguish his nature from the Godhead, and points to the true reading of a later verse in which Christ is called the mystery of God, even the Father, an unique and remarkable expression preparing for the understanding of the words that he who has seen the Son has seen the Father.

debates: What makes a saint: Gill denies birth, baptism and outward reformation and grounds it in eternal election, imputation and the sanctifying grace of the Spirit, where Clarke says in five words that they were those who professed Christianity and Wesley makes the word express union with God

How the city's name is spelled: Clarke prefers a different form from the received one on the authority of many manuscripts, versions and fathers and calls it most probably the true reading, while Robertson says only that the spelling is uncertain, the manuscripts differing between the title and the text

Whether the salutation named Christ: Ellicott accepts the shorter reading and finds theological significance in it, Robertson accepts it and notes that this is the only opening benediction without the name, and Clarke reports the omission but judges the evidence insufficient

What the letter from Laodicea was: Barnes takes the obvious sense to be a lost letter of Paul's to that church, notes that none is extant, and canvasses the opinions offered, beginning with the suggestion that the Laodiceans had written to Paul

Why the letter opens with thanks: Calvin's rule that thanksgiving stands in place of congratulation, teaching us to remember God's goodness in all our joys and to give thanks for what he confers on others, alongside Henry's broader rule that thanksgiving ought to be a part of every prayer
outliers: Robertson's quotation that the church at Colossae was the least important of any to which Paul's epistles were addressed, and his answer that Paul had no greater message for any church than the one he gives here concerning the Person of Christ

4.pericope_label: Faith, love and hope, the spread of the gospel, and the report of Epaphras

schools.summary: Gill takes the faith commended to be not only a hearty assent to the whole doctrine of Christ and a sincere profession of it but the grace of faith itself, the operation of the Spirit of God in the soul, which had not Moses nor any mere man but Christ for its object; he says the hope laid up in heaven was what encouraged their faith and enlarged their love; he marks the free grace of the gospel's coming, that they did not seek or inquire after it or go after it but it came to them, so that Christ was found of them who sought him not; and he distinguishes the love Epaphras reported from a carnal and worldly love, since they loved Paul for the spiritual grace that was in him and the spiritual usefulness he was of. Calvin says the phrase faith in Christ is used that we may always bear in mind that Christ is the proper object of faith, and that love to all the saints is named not to exclude others but because, in proportion as any one is joined to us in God, we ought to embrace him the more closely with special affection; he argues that the hope of eternal life will never be so inactive as not to produce love, since the man fully persuaded that a treasure of life is laid up for him in heaven will aspire thither and look down upon this world, meditation on the heavenly life stirring up our affections both to the worship of God and to exercises of love, and he warns that those who pervert the passage to extol the merits of works reason futilely, since it does not follow that because hope stimulates us to aim at upright living our salvation depends on works. On the spread of the gospel he guards the point that the faith of it does not depend on its success, as though a man should believe it because others believe it, and that though the whole world should fail and heaven itself should fall the conscience of a pious man must not waver, since God on whom it is founded remains true, though this does not hinder faith from being confirmed whenever it perceives God's excellence; and on the love in the Spirit he follows an earlier father in the sense while dissenting from him on the preceding words, saying that such love has no view to the world but is consecrated to the service of piety and has an internal root, where carnal friendships depend on external causes.

Clarke observes that the opening is very similar to that of the epistle to the Ephesians and that the Apostle seems to have considered the church at Ephesus and that at Colosse to have been nearly in the same state, the two epistles being very similar in their doctrine and phraseology; he turns the spread of the gospel into a figure, the doctrine a traveller whose object is to visit the whole habitable earth, who commenced his journey in Judea, proceeded through Syria and the different parts of Asia Minor, has lately arrived at their city everywhere proclaiming glad tidings, and is so rapid in his course that he has already gone nearly through the countries under Roman dominion and will travel on till he has proclaimed his message to every people; he reports on Epaphras that some think him the same as Epaphroditus, the one being a contraction of the other as Demas is of Demetrius, notes that one version actually reads the longer name here, holds that he was a Colossian who became a deacon of that church, and reports the opinion that he was the first who preached the gospel there; and on the love reported he says the heavenly flame in the heart of this minister communicated itself to those who heard him, like priest like people, and that Epaphras gave full proof of their love not only by describing it but by presenting the supplies it had furnished. Wesley notes that Paul had written to them before, and that the word of truth means the true gospel preached to them, and glosses their knowing the grace of God in truth as a true experience of the gracious power of God.

Barnes answers at once that Paul's saying he heard of their faith does not prove he had never been at Colosse or did not establish the church there, since he uses a similar expression of the Ephesians, whose founder he undoubtedly was; he takes hope for the thing hoped for and makes the faith and love he had heard of the evidence that such a hope was theirs, since where there is such faith and love there is a well-founded hope of heaven; he says the object of the sixth verse is to excite in them a sense of gratitude that the gospel had been sent to them, being confined to no place or people but designed to be a universal religion offering the same blessedness to all; and he makes Epaphras a minister of the church at Colosse, probably sent to consult Paul on its affairs, while denying that there is any evidence he was its founder, and takes the love reported to have been wrought in them by the Holy Spirit and not mere natural affection. Ellicott insists that the words rendered for the hope really mean on account of the hope, so that faith and love are spoken of not merely as leading up to hope but as actually kindled by it, and calls the place assigned to hope in this passage notable; he says the received text of the sixth verse is certainly incorrect, gives the probable reading, and draws two lessons from it, the universality of the gospel, in which it stands contrasted with all local and national religions, whether of Judaism or of Paganism, and equally with the secret doctrines of Gnostic speculation, intelligible only to the initiated few, and the test of its reality by practical fruit; on Epaphras he allows that the name is a shortened form of the longer one but calls it most unlikely that he is the same man as the Epaphroditus of the epistle to the Philippians, makes him apparently a native of the city and apparently its first evangelist, whose work could not have been transient, and notes that his coming was to give account of his deputed work; and he glosses the love in the Spirit as love in the grace of the Holy Ghost, especially love towards Paul. Robertson says the report came from Epaphras and calls the plural literary unless Timothy is included, leaves open whether the phrase about hope attaches to the giving of thanks or, as he thinks likelier, to the love just before, observes that hope is here objective, the goal ahead, and that the participle means laid away or by, the word used of the pound laid away in a napkin; he calls the phrase in all the world a legitimate hyperbole, since the gospel was spreading all over the Roman empire, notes that the periphrastic tenses emphasise the continuity of the process and that the growing and the fruit-bearing go on simultaneously, as always with Christians, inward growth and outward expansion together; and he settles a smaller point on Epaphras, that the true reading is on our behalf and not on yours, so that in a true sense he was Paul's messenger to Colosse.

debates: Whether hearing of their faith proves Paul had never been at Colosse: Barnes denies it from the parallel with the Ephesians, whose founder he undoubtedly was, while Clarke uses the same parallel to argue that the two churches were in nearly the same state

What hope is doing in the sentence: Ellicott insists it means on account of the hope, so that faith and love are kindled by it rather than leading to it, Robertson leaves the connection open and prefers the link with love, Barnes takes hope for the thing hoped for and makes faith and love its evidence, and Calvin warns against perverting it to extol the merits of works

Whether Epaphras founded the church, and whether he is Epaphroditus: Barnes denies the founding, Ellicott makes him apparently the city's first evangelist while calling the identification most unlikely, and Clarke reports both the identification, with a version that reads the longer name here, and the opinion that he first preached there

Whether faith depends on the gospel's success: Calvin denies it flatly, since though the whole world should fail and heaven itself should fall the conscience of a pious man must not waver, while allowing that faith is confirmed when it perceives God's excellence in the spread
outliers: Clarke's figure of the gospel as a traveller who commenced his journey in Judea and has already gone nearly through the countries under Roman dominion
Ellicott's contrast of the gospel's universality with all local and national religions and equally with the secret doctrines of speculation, intelligible only to the initiated few
Calvin's warning that hope stimulating us to upright living does not make salvation depend on works
Calvin's line that though the whole world should fail and heaven itself should fall the conscience of a pious man must not waver
Robertson's note that the growing and the fruit-bearing go on simultaneously, as always with Christians, inward growth and outward expansion together
Robertson's rendering of the participle as laid away or by, the word used of the pound laid away in a napkin
Gill's observation that they did not seek or inquire after the gospel but it came to them
Clarke's summary of the ministry at Colosse, like priest like people

9.pericope_label: The prayer for knowledge, for a worthy walk, and for strength unto patience

schools.summary: Gill takes the cause of the prayer from all that precedes, their faith, their love and the good hope of eternal happiness; he says knowledge without practice is of no avail, so that Paul asks first knowledge and then practice, since men cannot act according to the will of God unless they know it and should not rest in their knowledge when they have it; and on the prayer for strength he says believers are weak in themselves and insufficient of themselves to do or bear anything, standing in need of all kinds of spiritual might proportioned to the services and temptations they are called to. Calvin says that the more conspicuous the grace of God is in any, the more we ought specially to love and esteem them and be concerned for their welfare; that the end for which we make proficiency in God's school is that it may be manifest in our life that we have not been taught by God in vain, and that whoever does not direct his endeavours to this object may toil and labour much yet do nothing better than wander about in endless windings without making progress; and that the turn to strength puts them in mind of their own weakness, since they will not be strong otherwise than by the Lord's help, and magnifies grace the more, so far is any man from standing by dependence on his own strength that the power of God shows itself illustriously in helping our infirmity, believers being constantly exercised with the cross while a thousand temptations daily present themselves, so that they must arm themselves with an admirable patience.

Henry observes that Paul heard they were good and prayed that they might be better, and that though he could perhaps hear of them but seldom he prayed for them constantly; he insists on the practical side of the petition, that the knowledge of our duty is the best knowledge, that a mere empty notion of the greatest truths is insignificant, and that our knowledge of the will of God must always be practical, since we must know it in order to do it; and he adds that our knowledge is then a blessing indeed when it is in wisdom, when we know how to apply our general knowledge to our particular occasions and to suit it to all emergencies.

Clarke says nothing could satisfy the Apostle, for himself or his hearers, but the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of peace, since the Colossians had knowledge but it was their privilege to be filled with it, and as the bright shining of the sun in the firmament of heaven fills the whole world with light and heat so the light of the Sun of righteousness is to illuminate their whole souls; he warns that even a good work may be marred and rendered fruitless by being done improperly, out of season, or in a temper of mind that grieves the Holy Spirit, and lays out the exhortation in steps, to walk, to walk worthily, and to do everything unto all pleasing, that God might be pleased with the manner, the time, the motive and the object of every act; and he makes the joyfulness a continual testimony that they please God, and so a spring of perpetual comfort. Wesley confines the knowledge asked for to God's revealed will, glosses the wisdom as all the wisdom from above and the understanding as the power to discern by that light whatever agrees with or differs from his will, and calls the last petition the highest point, not only to know and to do and to suffer the whole will of God but to suffer it to the end, not barely with patience but with thankful joy.

Barnes says the progress they had already made and the love they had shown constituted an encouragement for prayer and a reason why higher blessings should be sought, since we always feel stimulated to pray for those who are doing well; he takes spiritual understanding for the understanding of those things that pertain to the Spirit, observes that God is pleased with those who desire to understand what he is and what he commands, and has made a world so beautiful as to invite us to contemplate his perfections; and he finds in the spirit with which Christians are enabled to bear up under trials a manifestation of power that shows it is not of human origin, the power being the power of his glory. Ellicott distinguishes the two verbs, the first being the general word for worship and the second prayer properly so called, asking from God what is requisite; he takes the noun for a full knowledge, to be attained in measure here and made perfect in heaven, and presses that the knowledge prayed for is knowledge of God's will and not speculation as to the nature of God, nor as to emanations from Deity, nor even as to the reasons of his mysterious counsels; on the walk he says the word rendered all pleasing is not found elsewhere in the New Testament but is used in classic and Hellenistic Greek for a general disposition to please, a constant preference of the will of others before our own, and is safe as a guide of action only towards God, since otherwise it must bear the bad sense it usually has; and he renders the phrase for power as the strength of his glory, glory being God's manifestation of himself in love to man, contrasting this prayer with the parallel in the epistle to the Ephesians, which looks to knowledge of the love of Christ where this looks to power of endurance of trial and suffering, and noting that the patience meant is endurance rather than what we usually call patience, illustrated by the typical example of Job. Robertson makes the word for knowledge the keynote of Paul's reply to the conceit of a false wisdom and says the cure for such intellectual upstarts is not ignorance and not obscurantism but more knowledge of the will of God; he adds that understanding is the faculty of deciding in particular cases where wisdom gives the general principles, that the word rendered all pleasing is late and usually means obsequiousness but stands here alone in the New Testament in a good sense which the papyri and inscriptions also carry, and quotes another that the end of all knowledge is conduct; and he notes that the word for might is applied in the New Testament only to God, and distinguishes the two graces, the one remaining under difficulties without succumbing, the other the long endurance that does not retaliate.

Chrysostom takes the cause of the prayer from what precedes, that because they had heard of their faith and love and had good hopes they were hopeful to ask for future blessings also, and draws the figure that as in the games we cheer on most those who are near upon gaining the victory, so Paul most exhorts those who have achieved the greater part; he notes that Paul prays not for one day nor two nor three, thereby showing his love while giving them a gentle hint that they had not yet arrived at the end; and he marks the prudence of the blessed Apostle, that he nowhere says they are destitute of everything but that they are deficient, which the words that ye may be filled everywhere show.

debates: What sort of knowledge is prayed for: Ellicott presses that it is knowledge of God's will and not speculation as to his nature, as to emanations from Deity, or as to the reasons of his counsels, Robertson makes the word the keynote of Paul's reply to a false wisdom and says the cure for intellectual upstarts is more knowledge and not ignorance, Henry insists that the knowledge of our duty is the best knowledge, and Wesley confines it to the revealed will

What the rare word for all pleasing means: Ellicott takes it for a general disposition to please, a constant preference of the will of others before our own, safe only towards God, and Robertson notes that it commonly means obsequiousness and stands here alone in the New Testament in a good sense

Why the prayer turns from knowledge to strength: Calvin says it puts them in mind of their own weakness and magnifies grace, since the power of God shows itself illustriously in helping our infirmity, Barnes finds in Christian endurance a power not of human origin, and Ellicott contrasts the parallel prayer in the epistle to the Ephesians, which looks to knowledge of the love of Christ where this looks to power of endurance

Why Paul prays so hard for those already doing well: Chrysostom's figure of cheering on in the games those nearest to victory, with the gentle hint that they had not yet arrived, Barnes's observation that we are always stimulated to pray for those doing well, and Calvin's rule that the more conspicuous the grace the more we ought to esteem them
