12.pericope_label: Thanks to the Father, the deliverance from darkness, and redemption in the Son

schools.summary: Gill notes that some versions and copies read God and the Father, and that the Father is such both to Christ by nature and to all his people by adoption, and that the words are spoken in the first person as the close of the petitions and the opening of the thanksgiving; on the deliverance he expounds the darkness as the power of Satan, who though once an angel of light is now darkness itself, whose kingdom is a kingdom of darkness and who blinds the minds of them that believe not, and observes that with the Jews one of the names of Satan is darkness; and he takes the redemption to lie in deliverance from all sin, from the law with its curse and bondage, and from the hands of Satan. Calvin says the delineation of Christ is begun here because this was the only remedy for fortifying the Colossians against all the snares by which the false apostles endeavoured to entrap them, to understand accurately what Christ was, since Christ alone makes all other things suddenly vanish, and there is nothing that Satan so much endeavours to accomplish as to bring on mists with a view to obscuring Christ, because he knows that by this means the way is opened up for every kind of falsehood, so that the only means of retaining as well as of restoring pure doctrine is to place Christ before the view such as he is with all his blessings. On the darkness he says that wherever God's grace is not there is nothing but darkness, that we ourselves are called darkness and afterwards the whole world and Satan the Prince of darkness, and that from this we may gather that the whole world, with all its pretended wisdom and righteousness, is regarded as nothing but darkness in the sight of God; and on the redemption he observes that the two nouns are placed together without a conjunction by way of explanation, so that redemption is the forgiveness of sins, since when God remits our transgressions he exempts us from condemnation to eternal death.

Henry says the passage is a summary of the doctrine of the gospel concerning the great work of our redemption, coming in not as the matter of a sermon but as the matter of a thanksgiving, since our salvation by Christ furnishes abundant matter of thanksgiving in every view of it; and he notices the order, that Paul does not discourse of the work of redemption in its natural order, for then he would speak of the purchase of it first and afterwards of the application, but here inverts the order because in our sense and feeling of it the application goes before the purchase, we first finding the benefits of redemption in our hearts and being then led by those streams to the original and fountain-head.

Clarke says the thanks are due because we have nothing but what we have received from God's mere mercy and can never claim anything from him on the score of merit; he renders the word for fitness as qualified, notes that some manuscripts and versions read called instead and that one great codex carries both readings, and takes the inheritance for a plain allusion to the division of the promised land by lot among the tribes, the lot being what belonged to a tribe and the portion what belonged to each family within it, the whole a type of the kingdom of God. On the darkness he says it is here personified and represented as having power, authority and sway, all who had not embraced the gospel being under it, and that nothing less than the power of God can redeem a man from it; and on the redemption he reports that the clause naming the blood is omitted by most manuscripts of weight and importance, by many versions and by most of the Greek fathers, and that an editor has left it out of the text, judges the reading probably not genuine, and adds at once that the Scriptures declare no other way of redemption than through the sacrifice of Christ, the same phrase standing without variation in the epistle to the Ephesians. Wesley says God made us meet for glory by justifying and sanctifying us, compresses the contrast of the thirteenth verse into a line, that power detains reluctant captives where a kingdom cherishes willing subjects, and makes forgiveness the beginning of redemption as the resurrection is the completion of it.

Barnes makes the thanksgiving itself another mode of walking worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, and holds that the word Father here refers not to God as the Father of his creatures but to the Father as distinguished from the Son, since it is the Father who is represented as the great Author of the whole plan of salvation and who translates us into the kingdom of the Son; he explains the word rendered translated as often used of removing a people from one country to another, citing a historian for the usage, and takes the last verse to prove that we obtain forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ while denying that it proves this to be all that we obtain through that blood. Ellicott calls the thankfulness here the thankfulness of humility, sensible that from the Father's love we have received all and can but receive, finds the verb for fitness used also of making men able ministers of the new covenant and refers it clearly to God's foreknowledge and call; on the deliverance he says the verb is rescued, properly applied to dragging a person out of battle or the jaws of danger, that the power of darkness is the power of evil, permitted to exist but in itself a usurped tyranny and not a true kingdom, and that the second verb is properly applied to the transplanting of races and the settlement of them in a new home, so that salvation, begun by rescue, is completed by the settlement of the rescued captives in the new kingdom of Christ. Robertson marks the transition at this point to the picture of the person and work of Christ in nature and grace and calls what follows a full and final answer to the depreciation of Jesus Christ by speculative philosophy and to all modern efforts after a reduced picture of him; he explains the noun for inheritance from the pebble or piece of wood first used in casting lots and then the allotted portion, quotes another for the sense that the share is situated in the kingdom of light, and explains redemption as a release on payment of a ransom for a slave or debtor, as the inscriptions show, with remission following it as a sending away.

debates: Why the doctrine comes as thanksgiving and in inverted order: Henry holds that the application goes before the purchase in our sense and feeling of it, Barnes makes the thanksgiving itself a mode of walking worthy, and Ellicott calls it the thankfulness of humility

Why Christ is set out at such length here: Calvin says it was the only remedy against the snares of the false apostles, since Satan's chief endeavour is to bring on mists obscuring Christ, and Robertson calls what follows a full and final answer to the depreciation of Christ by speculative philosophy and to all modern efforts after a reduced picture of him

Whether the clause naming the blood stood in the text: Clarke reports its omission by most witnesses of weight and judges the reading probably not genuine, while insisting the doctrine stands elsewhere, and Barnes reads the verse as proving forgiveness through that blood while denying that it proves forgiveness is all we obtain by it

What the fitness and the inheritance mean: Clarke takes the second for the division of the promised land by lot, tribe and family, Ellicott refers the first to God's foreknowledge and call, Robertson explains the noun from the pebble used in casting lots, and Wesley makes the fitness a matter of justifying and sanctifying
outliers: Calvin's account of Satan's chief endeavour, to bring on mists with a view to obscuring Christ, since by that means the way is opened up for every kind of falsehood
Calvin's conclusion that the whole world, with all its pretended wisdom and righteousness, is regarded as nothing but darkness in the sight of God
Robertson's phrase for what follows, a full and final answer to all modern efforts after a reduced picture of Christ
Wesley's epigram, that power detains reluctant captives where a kingdom cherishes willing subjects
Wesley's rule that forgiveness is the beginning of redemption as the resurrection is the completion of it
Henry's inversion, that we first find the benefits of redemption in our hearts and are then led by those streams to the original and fountain-head
Ellicott's note that the verb for delivered is properly used of dragging a person out of battle or the jaws of danger, and the verb for translated of transplanting races
Ellicott's description of the power of darkness as a usurped tyranny and not a true kingdom
The note in Gill and Calvin alike that one of the Jewish names for Satan is darkness

15.pericope_label: Christ the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of every creature

schools.summary: Gill sets out by degrees in what sense God is invisible: not to the Son who lay in his bosom, nor in some sense to the angels who always behold his face, but to men; not seen corporeally with the eyes of the body, though intellectually with the eyes of an enlightened understanding; not in his essence and nature, which is infinite and incomprehensible, but in his works of creation, providence and grace; and not immediately but mediately, in and through Christ, in whom he gives the light of the knowledge of the glory of his person, and even so not perfectly now but in the other state, when the saints shall see him face to face; and he adds that the image is of the Father, not to the exclusion of the Son or the Spirit, who are with him the one God. Calvin says the title means that it is in him alone that God, who is otherwise invisible, is manifested to us, and then rejects the patristic handling of the verse: he knows well how the ancients explained it, since having a contest to maintain with the Arians they insisted on the equality of the Son with the Father and on his consubstantiality, while making no mention of what is the chief point, in what manner the Father makes himself known to us in Christ; and as for laying the whole stress of the defence on the term itself, by contending that a creature cannot be said to be the image of the Creator, he calls that excessively weak, and holds it set aside by Paul's own application of the word to man.

Henry says that Christ in his human nature is the visible discovery of the invisible God, and that he who has seen him has seen the Father, so that we should adore these mysteries in humble faith and behold the glory of the Lord in Christ Jesus; and that he was born or begotten before all the creation, before any creature was made, which is the Scripture way of representing eternity and by which the eternity of God is represented to us.

Clarke calls the Son the counterpart of God Almighty and argues from the epithet that if this is the image of the invisible God then nothing that appeared in him could be that image, for what could be visible in the Son could be visible in the Father also; this is that form of God of which he divested himself, the ineffable glory whose essential nature he concealed, that inaccessible light which no created being can see. On the firstborn he takes the phrase for the same thing as the name given him which is above every name, so that he is as man at the head of all the creation of God, and denies that he can with any propriety be considered a creature, having himself created all things and existed before anything was made. Wesley divides the image by the two natures, that in his divine nature the Son is the invisible image and in his human the visible image of the Father; reads the firstborn as begotten before every creature, subsisting before all worlds, before all time, from all eternity; and says that by describing the glory of Christ and his pre-eminence over the highest angels the Apostle here lays a foundation for the reproof of all worshippers of angels.

Chrysostom presses the title hard, asking whose image we will have him be, and answering that if God's, then he is exactly like the one to whom we assign him; he asks why no angel is anywhere called either image or son while man is called both, and answers that in the one case the exaltedness of their nature might presently have thrust the many into impiety, whereas the mean and low nature of man is a pledge of security against it and will not allow any, even should they desire it, to bring down the Word so low, so that where the meanness is great the Scripture boldly asserts the honour, and where the nature is higher it forbears.

Barnes says the object of the passage, as in the parallel place in the epistle to the Ephesians, is to give a just view of the exaltation of the Redeemer, and that in both cases the design is probably to meet some erroneous opinion on the subject then prevailing in those churches or among those who claimed to teach there; he explains that the word properly denotes a copy or delineation which accurately and fully represents its object, in contradistinction from a rough sketch or outline, so that the being and perfections of God are accurately and fully represented by Christ. Ellicott says the clause needs the most careful examination and lays down two things: that the word is used in the New Testament for real and essential embodiment as distinguished from mere likeness, which he proves from four other places, including the contrast between a shadow of good things to come and the very image of the things, and the changing of us from glory to glory into the image of the glorified Christ; and that although Paul, speaking popularly, elsewhere calls man the image and glory of God, the allusion is to the passage which says with stricter accuracy that man was made after the image of God. Robertson calls Jesus the very stamp of God the Father as he was before the Incarnation and is now, sets the passage beside the great openings of the fourth Gospel and of the epistle to the Hebrews and beside the hymn in the epistle to the Philippians, and notes that the word firstborn can no longer be considered purely Biblical, since it is found in inscriptions and in the papyri, denying that its use bears the conclusion Arius drew from it.

debates: Whether the argument from the word image proves what the fathers made it prove: Chrysostom presses the title and asks why no angel is ever called image or son while man is called both, where Calvin holds that the ancients, contending with the Arians, insisted on equality and consubstantiality while omitting the chief point, and calls the stress laid on the term excessively weak since Paul himself applies the word to man

What the word image carries: Barnes takes it for a copy that accurately and fully represents, against a rough sketch, Ellicott for real and essential embodiment as distinguished from mere likeness, Robertson for the very stamp of the Father, and Clarke argues that nothing visible in the Son could be that image

In what sense God is invisible: Gill sets out four distinctions, not to the Son nor wholly to angels but to men, not corporeally but intellectually, not in essence but in his works, and not immediately but through Christ; Wesley and Henry divide it instead by the two natures

What firstborn of every creature means: Clarke makes it the name above every name and denies that he can be considered a creature, Wesley makes it begotten before every creature from all eternity, Henry calls it the Scripture way of representing eternity, and Robertson denies that the word bears the conclusion Arius drew from it
outliers: Chrysostom's rule that where the meanness is great the Scripture boldly asserts the honour, but where the nature is higher it forbears
Calvin's rebuke of the ancients, that in contending with the Arians they made no mention of the chief point, in what manner the Father makes himself known to us in Christ
Clarke's argument that if the image were visible in the Son it could also be visible in the Father
Robertson's note that the word firstborn is found in inscriptions and in the papyri and can no longer be considered purely Biblical
Wesley's distinction, that in his divine nature the Son is the invisible image and in his human the visible image of the Father
Barnes's contrast between an image that accurately and fully represents its object and a rough sketch or outline
Wesley's account of why the passage stands here, that it lays a foundation for the reproof of all worshippers of angels

16.pericope_label: All things created in him, and in him all things consist

schools.summary: Gill gives three reasons why the creation meant cannot be the new creation: whenever that is spoken of the word new is used or something equivalent, which is not the case here; all things in heaven are said to be created, and the sun and moon and stars are not capable subjects of a new creation; and to restrain the heavenly things to angels will not do either, since those who kept not their first estate find no place there any more and are never renewed, while the good angels, having never sinned, stand in no need of renovation. On the priority he allows both senses together, that Christ is before all things in dignity, being preferable to angels and men in his nature, names, offices and works, and before them in existence, as he must needs be since they are all made by him, being before the angels were in being or the heavens and the earth or any creature was formed, and therefore God, who is from everlasting to everlasting. Calvin prefers to understand by the first of the four names the heavenly palace of God's majesty, which we are not to imagine to be such as our mind can conceive of but such as is suitable to God himself, since we see the sun and moon and the whole adorning of heaven while the glory of God's kingdom is hid from our perception, being spiritual and above the heavens, that seat of blessed immortality which is exempted from all change; and he subjects the angels to Christ, that they may not obscure his glory, on four grounds, that they were created by him, that their creation ought to be viewed as having a relation to him as its legitimate end, that he existed always prior to their creation, and that he sustains them by his power and upholds them in their condition, and he affirms this not of angels only but of the whole world.

Clarke reduces the two verses to four assertions: that Jesus Christ is the Creator of the universe, of all things visible and invisible, of all things that had a beginning, whether they exist in time or in eternity; that whatsoever was created was created for himself, he being the sole end of his own work; that he was prior to all creation and to all beings, whether in the visible or the invisible world; and that he is the preserver and governor of all things, since by him all things consist. Allowing St Paul to have understood the terms which he used, he concludes, the Apostle must have considered Jesus Christ as being truly and properly God, creation being the proper work of an infinite being. Wesley marks that the preposition denoting the beginning, the progress and the end is prior to the other two, that the pronoun, frequently repeated, signifies his supreme majesty and excludes every creature, and that the inhabitants of heaven are named rather than the house because they are more noble; he ranks the four orders, thrones above dominions and principalities above powers, and guesses that the two latter may express their office towards other creatures while the two former refer to God; and on the priority he presses the tense, that it is not said he was but he is, from everlasting to everlasting, adding that all things were and are compacted in him into one system, so that he is the cement as well as the support of the universe, and asking whether he is less than the supreme God.

Barnes says this is one of the reasons why Christ is called the image of God and the firstborn, since he makes God known by his creative power; the phrase used is universal, and Paul does not declare that Christ created all things in the spiritual kingdom of God or arranged the events of the gospel dispensation, as some have supposed, but that everything was created by him, so that there could not possibly be a more explicit declaration that the universe was created by Christ, and as if the simple declaration in the most comprehensive terms were not enough the Apostle goes into a specification of things existing in heaven and earth, as if to prevent the possibility of mistake. On the priority he reports that those who regard the creation as a moral one read the word as pre-eminence and not pre-existence, and answers that its fair and proper meaning is that he was before all things in the order of existence, which is equivalent to saying that he was eternal, and that the consisting means they are kept in their present state, their existence, order and arrangement continued by his power, so that if unsupported they would fall into disorder or sink back to nothing. Ellicott observes that Paul here takes up a phrase belonging only to Godhead and usually applied to the Father and distinctly applies it to Christ, with the significant change of from whom into in whom, the usual language of Scripture being from whom of the Father and through whom of the Son; on the priority he says both words are emphatic, that he and he only is while all else is created, that it is impossible not to refer to the I am of eternal existence claimed by our Lord for himself, and that the word should therefore be taken not of supreme dignity but of pre-existence; and he glosses the consisting as holding together in unity, obeying the primeval law of their being, attributing to our Lord not only the creative act but the constant sustaining power, which even less than the creative agency can be supposed to be a derivative and finite power, such as that of the Demiurge of Gnostic speculation. Robertson calls this central activity of Christ in the work of creation a complete denial of the Gnostic philosophy, notes that the perfect tense means the things stand created and remain created, so that the permanence of the universe rests on Christ far more than on gravity in what he calls a Christo-centric universe; and on the second verse he says the precedence of Christ in time and the pre-eminence as Creator are both stated sharply, that the verb means to cohere and hold together, that Christ is the controlling and unifying force in nature, and that the Gnostic philosophy that matter is evil and was created by a remote aeon is thus swept away, since the Son of God's love is the Creator and the Sustainer of a universe which is not evil.

Cyril turns the verse into a creed, confessing one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten Son of God, begotten of his Father very God before all worlds, by whom all things were made, since whether they be thrones or dominions or principalities or powers all things were made through him and of things created none is exempted from his authority; and he silences three parties with it, every heresy which brings in different creators and makers of the world, those who say that the sun is the Christ, since he is the sun's Creator and not the sun which we see, and those who say that the world is the workmanship of angels and so wish to steal away the dignity of the Only-begotten. He adds that Christ reigns over the things which have been made by him, not having seized another's spoils but reigning over his own workmanship, and that he is the Maker at the Father's bidding not only of the things which are seen but also of the things which are not seen.

debates: Whether the creation meant is the new creation: Gill denies it on three grounds, that the word new is always used, that the heavenly bodies are not capable subjects of it, and that it cannot be restrained to angels either, while Barnes denies that Paul speaks of the spiritual kingdom or the gospel dispensation at all

Whether the priority claimed is of dignity or of existence: Barnes reports the reading of pre-eminence and answers that the fair meaning is priority in the order of existence, Ellicott says it must be pre-existence and not supreme dignity, Wesley presses that it is not said he was but he is, and Gill allows both senses together

Against whom the passage is aimed: Cyril silences with it those who bring in different creators, those who say the sun is the Christ, and those who make the world the workmanship of angels, while Robertson and Ellicott name the later doctrine of evil matter and a remote aeon, and Clarke concludes from four assertions that Paul must have held Christ to be truly and properly God

What the first of the four heavenly names means: Calvin prefers the heavenly palace of God's majesty, warning that we are not to imagine it such as our mind can conceive, while Wesley ranks the four orders and guesses at their offices
outliers: Robertson's line that the permanence of the universe rests on Christ far more than on gravity, in what he calls a Christo-centric universe
Robertson's summary that the philosophy which makes matter evil and the work of a remote aeon is thus swept away
Cyril's threefold silencing, of those who bring in different creators, of those who say the sun is the Christ, and of those who make the world the workmanship of angels
Cyril's image of Christ reigning not by having seized another's spoils but over his own workmanship
Ellicott's observation that Paul takes up a phrase belonging only to Godhead and usually applied to the Father, changing from whom into in whom
Ellicott's note that the sustaining power can even less than the creative be supposed a derivative and finite thing
Wesley's summary that Christ is the cement as well as the support of the universe, with his question whether he is less than the supreme God
Calvin's picture of the glory of God's kingdom hid from our perception, being spiritual and above the heavens
Barnes's observation that, as if the most comprehensive terms were not enough, the Apostle goes into a specification as if to prevent the possibility of mistake

18.pericope_label: Head of the body, the fullness that dwells in him, and the reconciliation of all things

schools.summary: Gill says the church meant is not any particular congregated church but the whole election of grace, the general assembly of the firstborn, which Christ purchased with his blood and will at last present to himself without spot or wrinkle, compared to a human body because it is one, consisting of many members set in just symmetry and proportion, neither more nor fewer; and he notes that the word Father is not in the original text but is rightly supplied, since the Father is the one who makes the saints meet and translates them into the kingdom of his dear Son. Calvin settles the headship against a rival sense: he grants that some include many things under the term, and that Paul uses the same metaphor elsewhere for the vital energy diffused from a root through all the members, but holds that here the Apostle speaks chiefly of government, showing that Christ alone has authority to govern the Church, that on him alone believers ought to have an eye, and that on him alone the unity of the body depends, which he turns against those who claim a visible head besides. He makes the fullness a fullness of righteousness, wisdom, power and every blessing, since whatever God has he has conferred upon his Son that he may be glorified in him, and draws the practical rule that we must draw from that fullness everything good we desire for our salvation, because God has determined not to communicate himself or his gifts to men otherwise than by his Son; and on the reconciliation he says it is a magnificent commendation of Christ that we cannot be joined to God otherwise than through him, since our happiness consists in cleaving to God and nothing is more miserable than to be alienated from him, and that what is here ascribed to Christ belongs peculiarly to him, so that no portion of this praise may be transferred to any other.

Clarke observes that where the two preceding verses spoke of the divine nature of Jesus Christ the Apostle now speaks of his human nature, and shows how highly that is exalted beyond all created things, so that from him, as the man in whom the fullness of the Godhead bodily dwelt, all the mercy and salvation of the gospel is received; he makes him the first that ever resumed the natural life with the employment of all its functions, never to lose it again; he reports the alternative rendering of the nineteenth verse, that in him it seemed right that all fullness should dwell, taking the fullness to refer to the divine nature dwelling in the man Christ Jesus; and on the reconciliation he guards the direction of the enmity, that it was on the part of the creature, since God, though angry with the wicked every day, is never unwilling to be reconciled, while man, whose carnal mind is enmity against God, is naturally averse from this reconciliation, so that it requires the blood of the cross to atone for the sin and the influence of the Spirit to reconcile the transgressor. Wesley will have Christ head both of influence and of government to the whole body of believers, notes that the repeated form of words marks the entrance on a new paragraph, takes the beginning absolutely for the Eternal, and asks of the pre-eminence who can sound this depth; he says the fullness dwells in him constantly, as in a temple, and always ready for our approach to him; and he limits the heavenly side of the reconciliation to those now in paradise, the saints who died before Christ came, noting that the earthly is mentioned first because there the enmity began.

Barnes takes the beginning to mean that Christ is the fountain of authority and power alike in the work of creation and in the church, and denies that firstborn from the dead means literally that he was the first who rose, since he himself raised up Lazarus and others and the bodies of saints arose at his crucifixion, holding rather that he had the pre-eminence among them all; he supplies the word Father in the nineteenth verse and defends the supply from the earlier verse in which the Father is thanked for exalting the Son; and on the reconciliation he guards the timing, that the death did not actually effect peace but laid the foundation which would secure it. Ellicott says the pronoun is again emphatic, he who is the image of God being also the Head, and reports that an early father read here a kindred word, the first-fruits, calling the reading no doubt a gloss but an instructive one, since it shows the reference is to Christ as being in his humanity the first principle of the new life to us; on the nineteenth verse he calls the construction doubtful, canvasses the supply of either God or Christ, observes that Christ is the easier supply grammatically but accords ill with the invariable reference of all things, both by our Lord himself and by his Apostles, ultimately to the good pleasure of the Father, and judges the simplest construction to be that which takes the fullness itself for the subject; and on the reconciliation he marks the difference from the parallel epistle, where the treatment is fuller in bringing out the unity of Jew and Gentile with one another as well as with Christ, while this passage involves deeper and more mysterious teaching, since it includes not merely all humanity but all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Robertson takes the church here in the general sense and not of a local body, assembly or organization, and sets the contrast between the realm of nature in the preceding verses and the realm of spirit or grace in these; he notes that there is no word for the Father in the nineteenth verse though the verb calls for a subject, quotes another that the fullness is a recognised technical term in theology denoting the totality of the divine powers and attributes, and observes that where a later philosophy distributed those powers among various aeons Paul gathers them all up in Christ, in a full and flat statement of his deity; and he says the double compound verb for reconciling occurs only here, in a later verse of this chapter and in the parallel epistle, and nowhere else so far as is known, the addition being clearly for the idea of complete reconciliation, while the use of the phrase for the universe is as though it were somehow out of harmony.

Cyril states the dilemma that made the cross necessary: we were enemies of God through sin and God had appointed the sinner to die, so that one of two things must needs have happened, either that God in his truth should destroy all men or that in his loving-kindness he should cancel the sentence; but the wisdom of God preserved both the truth of his sentence and the exercise of his loving-kindness, Christ taking our sins in his body on the tree that we by his death might die to sin and live unto righteousness; and he adds that of no small account was he who died for us, since he was not a literal sheep, nor a mere man, nor even more than an angel merely, but God made man.

debates: What headship means here: Calvin grants the metaphor of vital energy diffused from a root but holds that Paul speaks chiefly of government, so that Christ alone governs the Church and on him alone its unity depends, where Wesley will have him head both of influence and of government

In what sense Christ is firstborn from the dead: Barnes denies any literal priority, since Christ himself raised others and saints arose at his crucifixion, Clarke makes him the first that resumed natural life never to lose it again, and Ellicott reports an early father's reading of first-fruits as a gloss but an instructive one

Who is the subject of it pleased, the word Father being absent from the Greek: Barnes supplies the Father from the earlier verse, Clarke reports the rendering that takes the fullness as subject, Ellicott calls the construction doubtful and judges that supply the simplest while rejecting Christ as ill according with the reference of all things to the Father, and Robertson notes only that the verb calls for a subject

How far the reconciliation reaches: Ellicott makes this passage deeper than the parallel epistle because it includes not merely all humanity but all things in earth and heaven, Robertson finds the phrase used as though the universe were somehow out of harmony, Wesley limits the heavenly side to the saints who died before Christ came, and Barnes holds that the death laid the foundation of peace rather than effecting it
outliers: Cyril's dilemma, that either God in his truth should destroy all men or in his loving-kindness cancel the sentence, and the wisdom of God preserving both the truth of his sentence and the exercise of his loving-kindness
Cyril's climax, that he who died for us was no literal sheep, nor a mere man, nor an angel, but God made man

Robertson's quotation that the fullness is a recognised technical term denoting the totality of the divine powers and attributes, with his contrast that where a later philosophy distributed those powers among aeons Paul gathers them all up in Christ
Robertson's note that the double compound verb for reconciling occurs only here, at a later verse and in the parallel epistle, and nowhere else so far as is known
Clarke's balance, that though God is angry with the wicked every day he is never unwilling to be reconciled, the aversion being wholly on man's side
Calvin's rule that we must draw from the fullness of Christ everything good we desire, since God has determined not to communicate himself or his gifts otherwise than by his Son
Wesley's note that the fullness dwells in him constantly, as in a temple, and always ready for our approach, and his question who can sound this depth

21.pericope_label: You that were alienated, reconciled in the body of his flesh, if ye continue in the faith

schools.summary: Gill applies the general blessing of reconciliation particularly to the Colossians, who were eminent instances of it, and takes their alienation to have been from the life of God and from living agreeably to his will; on the condition he answers that the virtue and efficacy of Christ's blood and the reconciliation of their persons did not depend on their faith or their abiding in it, but that faith and continuance in it were the necessary means of their presentation in unblemished holiness, so that the verse shows the necessity of the saints' final perseverance in faith. Calvin notices the turn from doctrine to persons, that the general doctrine is now applied particularly to them so that they may feel themselves guilty of very great ingratitude if they allow themselves to be drawn away from Christ to new inventions, and says the arrangement must be carefully observed, since the particular application of a doctrine affects the mind more powerfully, they being themselves a mirror of that grace which he had declared to be offered to mankind through Christ. On the body of his flesh he calls the expression in appearance absurd and takes it for that human body which the Son of God had in common with us, since he put on the same nature with us and took upon him this vile earthly body, subject to many infirmities, that he might be our Mediator and our brother, and by dying become a sacrifice that might make his Father propitious to us; and he adds that here we have the second and principal part of our salvation, newness of life, since the entire blessing of redemption consists mainly in remission of sins and spiritual regeneration.

Clarke explains the word for alienation as describing the state of the Gentiles, since where the Jews were at least by profession dedicated to God these were given up to others, worshipping not the true God but gods many and lords many, the compound signifying to estrange utterly and to be wholly the property of another; on the presentation he expounds the three words in turn, holy as saved from their sins, unblamable as filled with the Spirit and having the law written in their hearts so that love becomes the principle and motive of every action, the tree being good and the fruit therefore good also, and unreprovable as filled with love, joy, peace, meekness, gentleness and goodness, against which there is no law; and on the last clause he takes the hope of the gospel for the resurrection of the body and the glorification of body and soul together, and calls the phrase about every creature a Hebraism for the whole human race, particularly referring to its two grand divisions. Wesley says actual alienation of affection makes habitual enmity, that the mind covers both the understanding and the affections, and that the wicked works continually feed and increase inward alienation from and enmity to God; he distinguishes the body of his flesh from his body the church and makes it his entire manhood; and he divides the presentation three ways, holy toward God, spotless in ourselves, unreprovable as to our neighbour.

Barnes says the alienation was not merely by wicked works or an evil life but was seated in the mind and led to wicked works, a deliberate and purposed enmity, not the result of passion and excitement but having a deeper seat and taking hold of the intellectual powers; on the death he explains that it removed the obstacles to reconciliation on the part of God, vindicating his truth and justice and maintaining the principles of his government, and was also the means of bringing the sinner himself to a willingness to be reconciled; on the condition he says without qualification that it will be impossible to be saved unless we continue to lead lives becoming the gospel; and on the last clause he denies that it can be supposed that every creature under heaven had actually heard the gospel, taking the words rather of the design that it should be preached to every creature. Ellicott says they were not naturally aliens but estranged, and that the enmity of heart is not properly caused by wicked works but shown in them and probably intensified by reflex action through them; on the body of his flesh he says the meaning is of course his natural body as distinguished from his mystic body named above, but that this is no sufficient reason for the phrase, since no confusion between them was possible here, so that without ascribing to the word a distinctly polemical intention he supposes there was present to the Apostle's mind the thought of the Gnosticism which depreciated the body as evil and must always have inclined to the idea that Jesus Christ had not come in the flesh; and on the condition he says the particle conveys a supposition hardly hypothetical, if as I presume, if as I trust, since St Paul cannot refrain from needful warning but refuses to anticipate failure. Robertson describes the participle as a periphrastic perfect passive marking a continuing state of alienation and a vivid picture of heathenism, says plainly that Paul combines the two words for body and flesh to make plain the actual humanity of Jesus against an incipient Docetic denial of it, and reads the condition as one of the first class, determined as fulfilled, with a touch of eagerness in the particle, the saint being pictured as a building grounded on a foundation and as one seated firmly in a chair.

Chrysostom shows that Christ reconciled even those who were unworthy of reconciliation, and says the clause is added lest, on hearing of the power of darkness, we should consider it necessity; for it is not the same thing to deliver out of evils him that through necessity came to suffer and him that of his own will endures, since the former is worthy to be pitied but the latter hated, and yet these, who not against their wills nor from compulsion but with their wills and wishes sprang away from him and are unworthy of it, he has reconciled.

debates: Where the alienation was seated: Barnes makes it a deliberate and purposed enmity seated in the mind and taking hold of the intellectual powers, Ellicott says the enmity of heart is shown in wicked works and intensified by them rather than caused by them, Wesley that alienation of affection makes habitual enmity, and Chrysostom that they sprang away with their wills and wishes and not from compulsion

Why Paul writes the body of his flesh rather than simply his body: Ellicott supposes without ascribing a polemical intention that the philosophy which depreciated the body as evil was present to his mind, Robertson says plainly that the two words are combined against an incipient denial of Christ's humanity, and Calvin calls the expression in appearance absurd and takes it for the body he had in common with us

What the condition threatens: Gill answers that the efficacy of Christ's blood does not depend on their faith but that continuance is the necessary means of their presentation, so that the verse shows the necessity of final perseverance, Barnes says without qualification that it will be impossible to be saved unless we continue, and Ellicott and Robertson soften the particle instead, the one calling it a supposition hardly hypothetical and the other a condition assumed fulfilled

How far every creature under heaven reaches: Barnes denies that all can literally have heard and takes the words of the design, while Clarke calls the phrase a Hebraism for the whole human race and its two grand divisions
outliers: Chrysostom's distinction that it is not the same thing to deliver him who through necessity came to suffer and him who of his own will endures, the one worthy to be pitied and the other hated

Calvin's word to the Colossians that they are themselves a mirror of the grace he had declared to be offered to mankind, and his rule that the particular application of a doctrine affects the mind more powerfully
Clarke's contrast that where the Jews were at least by profession dedicated to God the Gentiles were given up to others, the compound signifying to be wholly the property of another
Clarke's gloss on the presentation, that the tree being good the fruit is also good
Wesley's threefold division, holy toward God, spotless in ourselves, unreprovable as to our neighbour
Robertson's two metaphors for the settled believer, a building grounded on a foundation and a man seated firmly in a chair
Calvin's summary that the entire blessing of redemption consists mainly in remission of sins and spiritual regeneration
Ellicott's rendering of the particle, if as I presume, if as I trust, since the Apostle refuses to anticipate failure

24.pericope_label: Filling up the afflictions of Christ, the ministry committed to Paul, and the mystery now revealed

schools.summary: Gill observes that as soon as the Apostle mentions his being a minister of the gospel he speaks of his sufferings, since those always attend such an office, being appointed by God, foretold by Christ, necessary and to be patiently endured, and notes that he wrote this epistle in his bonds at Rome, not for any crime but for Christ's sake and for the sake of the churches; and on the mystery he says the term marks off the gospel from the Scriptures at large, some of which are historical, some prophetical, some practical, and that the gospel is so called because it contains things which, though revealed, are mysteries to a natural man, while even to the enlightened, who have the clearest view of them, the manner of them cannot be accounted for. Calvin gives the purpose of the passage, that Paul provides against the honour of his apostleship being detracted from by the bonds and persecutions he endured for the sake of the gospel, since Satan perversely turns such things into occasions of rendering the servants of God the more contemptible, and that he encourages the Colossians by his own example not to be intimidated by persecutions; and on the ministry he sharpens the distinction with a phrase he takes from an early father, that Paul is a servant not to the price of redemption but to the preaching of it, the Apostles serving God and Christ for the advancement of the glory of both and serving the Church with a view to promote salvation, so that the two ministries differ in reason though the one cannot subsist without the other.

Henry says that both the sufferings of the Head and of the members are called the sufferings of Christ and make up, as it were, one body of sufferings, but that he suffered for the redemption of the church while we suffer on other accounts, since we do but slightly taste that cup of afflictions of which Christ first drank deeply; and that a Christian may be said to fill up what remains of the sufferings of Christ when he takes up his cross and, after the pattern of Christ, bears patiently the afflictions God allots to him.

Clarke reads the clause of Paul's own course, that he had still some afflictions to pass through before his race of glory should be finished, and traces his persecutions, so far as the Jews were concerned in them, to his asserting that God had chosen the Gentiles and called them to enjoy the very same privileges as the Jews and to constitute one Church with them, for which they attempted his life at Jerusalem and forced his appeal to Caesar; on the ministry he says Paul had received especial commission to preach salvation to the Gentiles according to the gospel economy, and takes the last phrase for fully preaching the doctrine of God, noting that on the common meaning of the word it would signify to accomplish the purpose of God as predicted by the prophets. Wesley makes the clause mean what remains to be suffered by Christ's members, and explains why such sufferings bear his name, because the suffering of any member is the suffering of the whole and of the head especially, which supplies strength, spirits, sense and motion to all, and because they are borne for his sake and for the testimony of his truth; and he guards it at once, that they are necessary for the church not to reconcile it to God or satisfy for sin, which Christ did perfectly, but for example to others, for the perfecting of the saints and the increasing of their reward.

Barnes takes the clause for what Paul lacked of coming up to the sufferings which Christ endured in the cause of the church, he suffering in the same cause, and traces his trials at Rome to his maintaining that the wall of partition between Jews and Gentiles was broken down and the gospel to be preached indiscriminately to all mankind; he explains the dispensation as the arrangement God had made, by which the gospel should be preached to the Gentiles, takes the last phrase for fully teaching and promulgating the gospel, and says the great doctrine that salvation was to be proclaimed to all mankind had been concealed for many generations and was therefore called a mystery or hidden truth, communicated especially to the apostles appointed to proclaim it and through them to all the saints. Ellicott notes that in the true reading there is no relative pronoun, so that the sentence starts with emphatic abruptness, and that in all three epistles of the captivity the same rejoicing is declared in himself and urged on his brethren; he observes that a little before Paul called himself a minister of the gospel and here a minister or servant of the Church, whereas elsewhere he is always the minister of God and of Christ, the Church being named here as the Body of Christ and so indissolubly united with him; and he takes the last phrase for fully preaching the word of God, to be a messenger of the perfect revelation which had now unfolded what was previously a hidden mystery. Robertson works from the word, a very rare double compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, meaning to fill up in turn, and says it is now Paul's turn, borrowing a figure from the playing field, Christ having had his turn, the grandest of all, and having suffered for us all in a sense not true of any one else, and yet not having caused suffering to cease, so that there is plenty left for Paul and for each of us in his time; he calls the ministry God's stewardship, by which Paul was made a minister of Christ, and the last phrase a fine one for a God-called preacher, to fill full or to give full scope to the word of God, adding that the preacher is an expert on that word by profession.

Chrysostom says the Apostle, having shown the lovingkindness of God and the honour by the greatness of the things given, introduces yet another consideration that heightens them, namely that before us no one knew it at all, as he writes also to the Ephesians, that neither angels nor principalities nor any other created power knew it but only the Son of God; and he notes that Paul says not simply that it was hid but that it was quite hid, and that even if it has but now come to pass yet it is of old, since from the beginning God willed these things and they were so planned out.

debates: What it means to fill up what is behind of the afflictions of Christ: Barnes takes it for what Paul lacked of coming up to Christ's sufferings in the same cause, Clarke for afflictions still to pass through before his race is finished, Wesley for what remains to be suffered by Christ's members, expressly not to reconcile the church or satisfy for sin, Henry for taking up the cross after Christ's pattern, and Robertson for Paul's turn in a succession that Christ began without ending suffering

In what sense Paul is minister of the Church: Ellicott marks the change from minister of the gospel and notes that elsewhere he is always minister of God and of Christ, while Calvin distinguishes the two grounds with an early father's phrase, a servant not to the price of redemption but to its preaching, and Robertson calls it God's stewardship

What it is to fulfil the word of God: Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all take it for fully preaching rather than accomplishing a prediction, Clarke noting what the common meaning of the word would give, and Robertson calling it a fine phrase for a God-called preacher

Why the gospel is called a mystery: Gill says because it contains things which even when revealed remain mysteries to a natural man, Barnes because the doctrine of a salvation proclaimed to all mankind had been concealed for generations, and Chrysostom because before us no one knew it at all, not even angels or principalities
outliers: Robertson's figure of Paul's turn, taken from the playing field, with Christ having had his turn, the grandest of all
Robertson's remark that the preacher is an expert on the word of God by profession
Wesley's guard, that the sufferings of the members are necessary not to reconcile the church or satisfy for sin but for example, for the perfecting of the saints and the increasing of their reward
Henry's image that we do but slightly taste the cup of afflictions of which Christ first drank deeply
Calvin's borrowed phrase, that Paul was a servant not to the price of redemption but to the preaching of it
Calvin's note that Satan perversely turns a servant's bonds into occasions of rendering him the more contemptible
Ellicott's observation that the true text has no relative pronoun, so that the sentence starts with emphatic abruptness
Chrysostom's distinction that Paul says not simply hid but quite hid, and that not even angels or principalities knew it

27.pericope_label: Christ in you the hope of glory, warning and teaching every man, and the labour it cost

schools.summary: Gill denies four grounds in the men themselves for the manifestation of the mystery: it was not their works, since God does not call them according to these but according to his own grace, nor any preparation or disposition in them towards the gospel, of which there is naturally none but all the reverse, nor a foresight of their better improvement of it, since that is not the method of divine grace, as the instances of Sodom and Gomorrha and of Tyre and Sidon witness, nor any holiness in them, since they became holy by the power of divine grace afterwards; he takes Christ and him crucified to have been the subject of the apostles' ministry, on which they dwelt and which was blessed for the conversion of sinners and the planting of churches; and he says the end of the labour was that in the great day of account Paul might bring a large number and set them before Christ as the seals of his ministry. Calvin puts a bridle on the presumption of men, that they may not allow themselves to be wise or to inquire beyond what they ought, but may learn to rest satisfied with this one thing, that it has so pleased God, whose good pleasure ought to be perfectly sufficient for us as a reason; and he says this is said principally for commending the grace of God, since Paul intimates that mankind by no means furnished occasion for God's making them participants of this secret, it being customary with him to place the good pleasure of God in opposition to all human merits and external causes. On the preaching he says Paul applies to his own ministry everything he has declared about the wonderful and adorable secret of God, with a view to adorn his apostleship and claim authority for his doctrine, and that it was not without good reason that he had noted a little before that Christ is the sum of that secret, that they might know nothing can be taught that has more of perfection than Christ.

Clarke draws out the verse as the sum and substance of the Apostle's preaching: he preached Christ as the only Saviour of sinners, and proclaimed this Christ as being in them, since the design of the gospel is to put men in possession of the Spirit and power of Christ, to make them partakers of the divine nature and so to prepare them for an eternal union with himself; and he says God manifests to these how abundantly glorious the gospel is among the Gentiles, and how effectual the doctrine of Christ crucified is for the salvation of multitudes. Wesley reduces the mystery to a phrase, Christ dwelling and reigning in them, which is the ground of their hope; and on the ministry he reverses the usual order outright, that we teach the ignorant and admonish them that are already taught.

Barnes explains that God willed to make this known, it having been concealed in his bosom until he chose to reveal it to his apostles, and that the truth that the gospel was to be preached to all mankind is one abounding in glory; on the ministry he takes issue with the English word for warning, since it commonly means to caution against danger whereas the Greek means to put in mind, to admonish and to exhort, so that the Apostle's business was to bring the offers of the gospel fairly before the mind of every man, as it had the same claims on all; and on the labour he says the word means agonizing, that Paul taxed all his energies as the wrestlers strove for the mastery in the Grecian games, and yet not by his own strength but by the power which God alone can give. Ellicott calls the willing emphatic, of God's own pleasure and inscrutable to man, and compares the fuller definition of the mystery in the parallel epistle, that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs and of the same body; on the ministry he says that in warning is implied the reproof of folly or sin while teaching is simply the instruction of those already warned, and suggests that the word rendered perfect may here carry the sense it bears elsewhere of one initiated in a mystery, so that against the exclusive claim of perfection made by the speculators in mystic knowledge the Apostle would present every man, learned or ignorant alike, perfect before God, in which universality of privilege lies the glorious distinction of the gospel. Robertson says God willed this change from hidden mystery to manifestation, calls the inclusion of the Gentiles in redemptive grace the crowning wonder to Paul, who feels the high honour keenly and meets the responsibility humbly; and he notes that the verb for proclaiming means to announce far and wide, that the phrase for every man stands three times over in opposition to a doctrine of intellectual exclusiveness, and that warning is about practice where teaching is about doctrine and calls for all wisdom.

debates: Which comes first, warning or teaching: Ellicott makes warning the reproof of folly or sin and teaching the instruction of those already warned, Wesley reverses it outright, that we teach the ignorant and admonish those already taught, Robertson divides them by subject rather than sequence, and Barnes denies that the word means warning of danger at all

Why God made the secret known: Calvin puts a bridle on presumption and rests everything on the good pleasure of God, Gill denies four grounds in the men themselves, Ellicott calls the willing inscrutable to man, and Robertson makes the inclusion of the Gentiles the crowning wonder to Paul

Against whom every man is repeated: Robertson notes the threefold repetition against a doctrine of intellectual exclusiveness, and Ellicott suggests that perfect may carry the sense of one initiated in a mystery, so that against the speculators in mystic knowledge the Apostle would present every man, learned or ignorant, perfect before God

What Christ in you amounts to: Clarke makes it the sum of the Apostle's preaching and the design of the gospel to make men partakers of the divine nature, Wesley reduces it to Christ dwelling and reigning in them, and Ellicott compares the fuller definition in the parallel epistle
outliers: Calvin's bridle on presumption, that the good pleasure of God ought to be perfectly sufficient for us as a reason
Gill's four denials, with the appeal to Sodom and Gomorrha and to Tyre and Sidon against any foresight of better improvement
Robertson's note that Paul feels the high honour keenly and meets the responsibility humbly
Ellicott's remark that in this universality of privilege lies the glorious distinction of the gospel
Barnes's correction that the word rendered warn does not mean warning of danger but putting in mind
Barnes's image of the wrestlers striving for the mastery in the Grecian games
Clarke's account of the design of the gospel, to make men partakers of the divine nature and prepare them for an eternal union with Christ
Calvin's note that nothing can be taught that has more of perfection than Christ
